title: Tunick v. Safir — three procedural decisions
lead: A proposed nude photograph moved from a federal injunction to certified state-law questions, the state court’s refusal to answer, and renewed limited federal relief. The judges agreed on some procedural steps for sharply different reasons.

actors.name: Spencer Tunick
actors.role: Photographer seeking protection for a brief nude-model shoot

actors.name: New York City
actors.role: Authority threatening interference under public-exposure laws

actors.name: Judges Calabresi, Sack, and Van Graafeiland

proceedings: District court enjoined interference July 16, 1999; Second Circuit stayed it July 17.
March 24, 2000 federal decision certified questions; New York Court of Appeals declined May 12.
May 19 federal decision dissolved stay and remanded for limited renewed injunction; fuller separate writings followed July 11.
limits: Three distinct decisions. No definitive state construction or final blanket constitutional right to public nudity. Injunction protected completion of photography, not later prosecution; Calabresi’s six-factor reasoning lacked panel-wide assent.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A five-minute photograph encounters the exposure law
paragraphs: Photographer Spencer Tunick planned an abstract arrangement of seventy-five to one hundred nude models on lower Manhattan’s Madison Street early Sunday, July 18, 1999. His otherwise identical applications proposed either clothed or nude models. New York City approved the clothed version and refused the nude one. Five earlier nude sessions had produced arrests, with charges ultimately dismissed. This photography would take no more than five minutes between 5:30 and 6:30 a.m.

Tunick sued July 13. Judge Harold Baer preliminarily enjoined interference July 16, finding protected art and a statutory exception. The Second Circuit stayed relief July 17 and heard expedited argument in September. The state exposure and promotion statutes exempted persons entertaining or performing in a play, exhibition, show, or entertainment. The City argued the exception required an indoor event with an audience. It abandoned licensing and time, place, and manner arguments on appeal; the injunction did not compel a permit.

sections.title: The federal panel asks the state court for guidance
sections.cue: March certification and three different positions
paragraphs: With conflicting municipal decisions and no controlling state appellate interpretation, the City favored certification and Tunick claimed the exception clearly applied. On March 24, 2000, Judges Calabresi and Sack certified whether the arrangement was exempt, whether any exemption required indoor activity, and whether a prohibition would be valid under New York’s Constitution. The panel retained jurisdiction and possible reconsideration of the stay; it decided neither statutory merits nor the final federal constitutional question.

Calabresi drew on abstention and constitutional avoidance. His six considerations concerned authoritative interpretation, importance and recurrence, avoidable constitutional problems, clarification, state sovereignty, and delay. Those were his analysis, not a panel test. He thought certification could resolve or clarify the dispute without turning federal courts into local permitting agencies. Continued plans for a future shoot and the prospect of guidance justified delay despite serious speech costs and possible mootness if the stay lifted. Dropped earlier charges made authoritative criminal interpretation uncertain.

Sack rejected that balance. Preventing expression under an unclear statute resembled unguided licensing. He favored immediate relief against prior restraint, while distinguishing arrest after the photograph; Tunick conceded he sought no immunity from later prosecution. Sack joined certification only because neither colleague supported his preferred relief and he saw it as the fastest practicable route.

Van Graafeiland would dismiss as moot because the complaint and injunction concerned the past July 18 date, leaving a new scheduled shoot for another case. He criticized delay and introducing an unraised state constitutional issue. Calabresi considered the controversy live because the intended photograph and threatened arrests persisted after the appellate stay prevented the event.

sections.title: New York declines to answer
paragraphs: The New York Court of Appeals unanimously declined the certified questions under its discretionary rule. Its per curiam opinion recognized certification’s general value but considered the added months of briefing and deliberation problematic in this delayed prior-restraint dispute. The federal court could lift its stay, permit photography, and potentially moot the questions while certification proceeded.

The parties also had never sought, briefed, or argued relief under New York’s Constitution. The state court would not responsibly decide that newly introduced issue. These combined concerns outweighed the ordinary benefits. Declining did not approve the photography, the statute, or the federal injunction; the questions remained unanswered.

sections.title: Limited federal protection resumes
paragraphs: On May 19 the Second Circuit held the preliminary injunction within discretion because Tunick showed irreparable injury and a clear likelihood of success. It dissolved the stay and remanded for a new date and a limited early-morning, nonbusiness-day injunction preventing arrests or interference until photography ended. The district court could minimize neighborhood intrusion, and intervening law making the event clearly illegal would qualify relief. Later arrests were not forbidden.

In his July concurrence, Calabresi predicted state law rather than automatically deciding the federal constitutional issue. Text and avoidance principles supported treating the arrangement as an exhibition without invented indoor or audience requirements. That preliminary prediction neither bound New York courts nor foreclosed later prosecution or reasonable regulation. Sack adhered to his earlier prior-restraint reasoning.

Van Graafeiland’s July dissent reported that a shoot occurred June 4 at another location and again urged dismissal as moot, criticizing a per curiam result resting on divergent rationales. His position did not alter the panel’s mandate dissolving the stay and directing limited renewed relief.
